text: Testing. Testing. Hello? Ah, there we go. Welcome to Camp Ashwood, the most expensive mistake I ever bought at a discount.
I'm Marty Bixby. I own this charming pile of lumber, and for tonight, you're my highly trained security division. Don't let that title go to your heads.
Here's the business model: I tear it down, somebody builds something profitable, and in the meantime you keep the local treasure hunters from walking off with the doorknobs.
Yep. Demolition. The land's worth more than the buildings, which is a sentence I should've checked before I signed anything.
That's your office. Fancy, right? Comes with four walls and absolutely no heating bill. Do not switch on the heater; the electrician says it builds character by catching fire.
Take a flashlight. Take the map. There's a generator behind the maintenance shed. Get that working and the security-side lights should come on. I emphasize should.

One other thing. People ask about the place's history. There was some ugly business a few years back. That's why it's empty. You're not here to write a documentary. You're here to keep people from stealing copper.
I bought a deed, not a scrapbook. Focus on the buildings that are still standing.
Okay, easy job. Find the fuse. Feed that antique dinosaur some fuel. Pull the starter. Then switch on the breaker marked SECURITY. In that order. I paid good money to have those labels put on.
Cabinet, left side of the shed. Little fuse box. If it's still there, congratulations, we've beaten the scavengers.
Something fell? In a fifty-year-old shed? Call the newspapers. Check no one got hurt and keep going.
Hey! Listen to that! She lives. The contractor told me that thing was scrap. Remind me to argue about his invoice.
There. Lights. See? Already making the place look less like a crime scene. Well, marginally.
Cabin Six. My favorite. Only one that came with the door pre-removed. Some idiot's been prying it open for souvenirs.
There's scrap lumber in the rack by the path. Fix that opening so someone can't just waltz inside. Make it ugly. We're tearing it down anyway.
Look at that, actual craftsmanship. You keep this up, I'll have you build me a house. On your own time, obviously.
That'll hold. Or at least it'll slow down anybody who doesn't own a crowbar.
Whoa. Are we securing a cabin or building a bank vault? Easy on my lumber, Rockefeller.
Almost done. Check the dining-hall latch, then circle back past the recreation court. If somebody's been in there, make a note. Don't go playing detective.
Oh, the court lights work? Great. Maybe I can sell those separately.
Sure, take a break. I'm only paying for a security shift, not Olympic training. Keep an eye on the fence while you're at it.
Yeah, exactly why I hired you. Folks want a little piece of spooky-camp history. I'll settle for them not stealing the plumbing.
You saw somebody? No? Then write down 'noise,' not 'intruder.' Big difference on an insurance form.
Something knocking? Probably boards settling. Which cabin?
...Six?  ...Okay. You secured that one, right?
Good. Then don't take it apart just to satisfy your curiosity. Head back to the office.
Nope. Don't touch it. Back to the office. Now.
I'm serious. We can send somebody in daylight. I am not explaining an injury to an attorney tonight.
Everybody back? Good. Now fill out the incident line. Properly. If that building collapses, I'd like the paperwork to say it was already thinking about it.
That's the sensible answer. Old buildings make old-building noises.
Fine. I'll have somebody check the locks tomorrow. In daylight. With a hard hat.
'Unknown.' Beautiful. Very reassuring. You really know how to make an owner feel great about his investment.
You did the job. Don't go back out there tonight. I'll call you in the morning.
